analysis.one_liner: Freezes major federal regulations until unemployment falls to 7.7% or lower.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no vote and no floor action, after 1 Republican senator introduced it and 28 more joined as cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred federal agencies from issuing any major new rule — including rules affecting the environment, public health and safety, and financial markets — until quarterly unemployment fell to 7.7% or below. The only automatic exception was for national security or a declared national emergency. It never got a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing costly new federal rules — banks implementing financial reforms, energy and chemical companies facing environmental rules, and other regulated industries — would gain years of delayed compliance costs while unemployment stayed above 7.7%.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing new federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any agency from taking a 'significant regulatory action' — one with a $100 million-plus annual economic effect or material effects on jobs, the environment, public health or safety — until the quarterly unemployment rate reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics is 7.7% or lower.

Provides only a narrow escape valve: the President can automatically waive the freeze solely for national security or a national emergency; any other waiver requires a presidential request to Congress and legislative action.

Gives any aggrieved party court review of agency actions taken in violation of the freeze, lets courts enjoin or strike those rules, and awards attorney fees to small businesses that substantially prevail.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost through rules that never get issued: weaker protections on air, water, workplace safety, consumer finance, and food and drug safety for as long as unemployment stays above the trigger. Workers harmed by unregulated practices, and small businesses that rely on fair rules of the road, pay along with everyone else.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The freeze applies no matter what a rule does: the definition of 'significant' sweeps in actions affecting the environment, public health or safety, and entitlement programs, so rules protecting workers and consumers would be blocked alongside ones imposing business costs.

Because the trigger is the unemployment rate, the moratorium could last for years and continues regardless of whether any specific rule is burdensome; in 2011 unemployment was well above 7.7%, so nearly every major rulemaking would have been frozen on day one.
The court challenge mechanism, with attorney fees paid to businesses that prevail even without a final judgment, invites litigation that can delay rules indefinitely even after the moratorium lifts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered regulated industries broad, multi-year relief from new rules, but did so by a blunt unemployment trigger rather than any case-by-case test of whether a rule was worth its cost. Rules that plainly protected public health and safety would have been frozen along with costly ones, and the only automatic exception was for national security or declared emergencies — leaving a poor trade for the public even if some rules did impose real compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Johnson introduced the bill on July 28, 2011, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
All 28 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat joined, and the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public came out ahead of where the bill would have put them: agencies kept their authority to issue health, safety, environmental, and financial rules during a period of high unemployment, and the industries hoping for a blanket freeze did not get one. Supporters of the bill gained nothing but a recorded position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, since agencies kept rulemaking

industries.industry: Regulated industries facing major new rules (energy, chemical, and manufacturing firms)
industries.note: The bill would have frozen environmental, health, and safety rulemaking for as long as unemployment stayed above 7.7%, delaying compliance costs for these industries. The public cost would be years of weaker air, water, and workplace protections during a weak economy.

Rules implementing post-2008 financial reforms qualify as 'significant regulatory actions' and would have been frozen, delaying consumer finance protections. Delayed rules meant delayed safeguards for borrowers and account holders.

The bill's attorney-fee provision lets small businesses recover legal costs when they successfully challenge rules issued in violation of the freeze. But small businesses also rely on rules that protect their workers, products, and market fairness, which the blanket freeze would also block.
